papers.abstract: Recently, there has been a trend to investigate the factual knowledge captured by Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs). Many works show the PLMs' ability to fill in the missing factual words in cloze-style prompts such as "Dante was born in [MASK]." However, it is still a mystery how PLMs generate the results correctly: relying on effective clues or shortcut patterns? We try to answer this question by a causal-inspired analysis that quantitatively measures and evaluates the wordlevel patterns that PLMs depend on to generate the missing words. We check the words that have three typical associations with the missing words: knowledge-dependent, positionally close, and highly co-occurred. Our analysis shows: (1) PLMs generate the missing factual words more by the positionally close and highly co-occurred words than the knowledge-dependent words; (2) the dependence on the knowledge-dependent words is more effective than the positionally close and highly co-occurred words. Accordingly, we conclude that the PLMs capture the factual knowledge ineffectively because of depending on the inadequate associations.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: ACE: Attribution-Controlled Knowledge Editing for Multi-hop Factual Recall
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing for multi-hop factual recall in LLMs be improved by understanding and leveraging internal neuron-level mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACE, a knowledge editing framework that uses neuron-level attribution to identify and edit query-value pathways, improving multi-hop factual recall.
papers.conclusion: ACE provides a mechanistically grounded solution for multi-hop knowledge editing and establishes a new pathway for advancing KE capabilities based on understanding internal reasoning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs store semantically analogous knowledge in structurally similar transformer components, with query and value neurons for specific knowledge types exhibiting consistent localization patterns.
During multi-hop reasoning, implicit subjects function as query neurons that sequentially activate corresponding value neurons across layers to accumulate information toward the final answer.
ACE outperforms state-of-the-art KE methods by 9.44% on GPT-J and 37.46% on Qwen3-8B in multi-hop accuracy.
Ablating query layers causes a 16.51% performance drop, while omitting value layers leads to a 40.45% decrease, demonstrating the necessity of both components.
GPT-J maintains fixed layer separation for query and value neurons, while Qwen3-8B exhibits dynamic, domain-specific alignment.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on FFN layers and does not edit attention heads, which may limit editability for some knowledge types.
Attribution mechanism relies on first-order Taylor approximation, potentially missing higher-order interactions.
Requires forward passes to compute importance scores, adding computational overhead.
future_direction: Integrating attention head editing into the ACE framework.
Developing more efficient attribution algorithms to reduce computational overhead.
Extending ACE to other model architectures and tasks beyond factual recall.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require efficient knowledge editing (KE) to update factual information, yet existing methods exhibit significant performance decay in multi-hop factual recall. This failure is particularly acute when edits involve intermediate implicit subjects within reasoning chains. Through causal analysis, we reveal that this limitation stems from an oversight of how chained knowledge is dynamically represented and utilized at the neuron level. We discover that during multi hop reasoning, implicit subjects function as query neurons, which sequentially activate corresponding value neurons across transformer layers to accumulate information toward the final answer, a dynamic prior KE work has overlooked. Guided by this insight, we propose ACE: Attribution-Controlled Knowledge Editing for Multi-hop Factual Recall, a framework that leverages neuron-level attribution to identify and edit these critical query-value (Q-V) pathways. ACE provides a mechanistically grounded solution for multi-hop KE, empirically outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 9.44% on GPT-J and 37.46% on Qwen3-8B. Our analysis further reveals more fine-grained activation patterns in Qwen3 and demonstrates that the semantic interpretability of value neurons is orchestrated by query-driven accumulation. These findings establish a new pathway for advancing KE capabilities based on the principled understanding of internal reasoning mechanisms.

papers.title: Facts in Stats: Impacts of Pretraining Diversity on Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: How does the diversity of pretraining data (in terms of contextual variation) impact the generalization of language models in learning both statistical patterns and factual associations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a synthetic testbed to study how pretraining diversity affects generalization, finding that diversity impacts in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance differently depending on contextual structure, and identifies optimization bottlenecks in embedding and unembedding layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, the synthetic framework allows isolation of effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Higher diversity can slow in-distribution factual recall while leaving in-distribution statistical accuracy largely unaffected.
Out-of-distribution effects depend on contextual structure: low diversity can severely impact factual recall, statistical accuracy, or both.
Data diversity introduces a cost-benefit dynamic: with limited training time, intermediate diversity levels are optimal.
The learning dynamics of the statistical and factual streams are coupled: increased complexity in one stream delays learning of both.
Through targeted interventions, optimization bottlenecks for out-of-distribution generalization are localized to the embedding and unembedding layers.
future_direction: Characterizing how context diversity and model capacity reshape the in-distribution loss landscape
papers.abstract: Language models are pretrained on sequences that blend statistical regularities (making text fluent) with factual associations between specific tokens (knowledge of facts). While recent work suggests that the variability of their interaction, such as paraphrases of factual associations, critically determines generalization ability, we lack a systematic analysis of these impacts. This paper introduces a flexible synthetic testbed that combines a statistical stream of generic tokens with an abstract factual stream of source-target token pairs, enabling fine-grained control over their interaction. The design enables the independent control of diversity nature by manipulating stream composition (contextual structure) and the diversity level by varying which statistical streams each fact appears in. Through controlled experiments, we find that while higher contextual diversity delays in-distribution (ID) factual accuracy, its impact on out-of-distribution (OOD) factual generalization depends critically on contextual structure. In some cases, OOD performance follows the same trend as ID, but in others, diversity becomes essential for non-trivial factual recall. Even when low diversity prohibits factual recall, optimal diversity levels depend on training duration. Beyond factual recall failures, we identify structures where statistical generalization fails independently, and others where both capabilities degrade. This shows how the interplay between contextual design and diversity level impacts different generalization aspects. Further, through a series of controlled interventions on the model components, we trace the OOD failures to distinct optimization bottlenecks, highlighting the importance of the embedding and unembedding layers. Our synthetic framework allows us to isolate effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.

papers.title: Relation Also Knows: Rethinking the Recall and Editing of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the relation (not just the subject) contribute to factual knowledge recall in auto-regressive transformer LMs, and how can knowledge editing be performed to avoid the over-generalizing problem by considering both relation and subject?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel relation-focused interpretation of factual knowledge recall in transformer LMs, showing that relational knowledge is aggregated at the last relation token, and proposes the RETS editing method which modifies the MLP at this position with subject constraints to significantly alleviate the over-generalizing problem.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel relation-focused perspective on knowledge recall in transformer LMs and demonstrates that the RETS editing method effectively avoids the over-generalizing problem, breaking the domination of subject-focused editing for future research.
papers.key_findings:
The last relation token is the decisive position for processing relation information during knowledge recall, with MLP and MHSA sublayers being most active there.
Relation-related attributes are aggregated from early to middle-late layers at the last relation token, and the target object is extracted from this aggregated relational knowledge.
Existing subject-focused editing methods (e.g., ROME) suffer from over-generalizing because they edit at the last subject token, which is earlier than the completion of relation inference and cannot attend to the relation token.
The proposed RETS method, which edits the middle-late MLP layer at the last relation token with subject constraints, outperforms baselines by over 30% on the new R-Specificity metric while remaining competitive on other criteria.
Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the subject constraints in RETS, as their removal leads to a significant drop in specificity performance.
papers.limitation:
The design of the subject constraints for RETS is relatively simple and negatively affects the quality of text generations (Fluency and Consistency).
The method is only applicable to editing each factual association separately and does not scale to sequential or batched edits.
The work only focuses on the MLP sublayers for knowledge recall, and a more complete explanation might require investigating other components.
future_direction: In-depth studies on how subject information is combined into the relation representation.
Scaling the editing method to sequential or batched facts.
Investigating other model components beyond MLP for a more complete explanation of the inference mechanism.
papers.abstract: The storage and recall of factual associations in auto-regressive transformer language models (LMs) have drawn a great deal of attention, inspiring knowledge editing by directly modifying the located model weights. Most editing works achieve knowledge editing under the guidance of existing interpretations of knowledge recall that mainly focus on subject knowledge. However, these interpretations are seriously flawed, neglecting relation information and leading to the over-generalizing problem for editing. In this work, we discover a novel relation-focused perspective to interpret the knowledge recall of transformer LMs during inference and apply it on single knowledge editing to avoid over-generalizing. Experimental results on the dataset supplemented with a new R-Specificity criterion demonstrate that our editing approach significantly alleviates over-generalizing while remaining competitive on other criteria, breaking the domination of subject-focused editing for future research.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: Fact Recall, Heuristics or Pure Guesswork? Precise Interpretations of Language Models for Fact Completion
papers.research_question: How do interpretability methods like causal tracing and information flow analysis differ across distinct prediction scenarios (exact fact recall, heuristics, guesswork, generic language modeling) in language models for fact completion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISM, a method for constructing datasets to distinguish four prediction scenarios in fact completion, and shows that causal tracing and information flow analysis yield distinct patterns for each scenario, revealing different mechanisms for exact fact recall versus heuristics or guesswork.
papers.conclusion: The PRISM dataset and analyses provide a more nuanced understanding of fact completion in LMs, showing that interpretability methods must account for different prediction scenarios to avoid misleading conclusions.
papers.key_findings:
Exact fact recall shows a clear peak in averaged indirect effects at (last subject token, mid layer) MLP states, supporting previous conclusions about memory storage.
Guesswork and heuristics recall show a critical role of late last token position MLP sublayers, unlike exact fact recall.
Generic language modeling samples do not show the mid-layer MLP peak, indicating no memory access.
Combined samples of fact completion scenarios can misleadingly show the exact fact recall pattern, dominating other scenarios.
Information flow analysis reveals distinct patterns for each scenario, e.g., exact fact recall versus generic language modeling.
papers.limitation:
The approach is not intended to classify every instance into one of the four scenarios, but to produce high-quality examples of each one.
The samples and analysis are focused on the English language.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) can make a correct prediction based on many possible signals in a prompt, not all corresponding to recall of factual associations. However, current interpretations of LMs fail to take this into account. For example, given the query "Astrid Lindgren was born in" with the corresponding completion "Sweden", no difference is made between whether the prediction was based on knowing where the author was born or assuming that a person with a Swedish-sounding name was born in Sweden. In this paper, we present a model-specific recipe - PrISM - for constructing datasets with examples of four different prediction scenarios: generic language modeling, guesswork, heuristics recall and exact fact recall. We apply two popular interpretability methods to the scenarios: causal tracing (CT) and information flow analysis. We find that both yield distinct results for each scenario. Results for exact fact recall and generic language modeling scenarios confirm previous conclusions about the importance of mid-range MLP sublayers for fact recall, while results for guesswork and heuristics indicate a critical role of late last token position MLP sublayers. In summary, we contribute resources for a more extensive and granular study of fact completion in LMs, together with analyses that provide a more nuanced understanding of how LMs process fact-related queries.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Online Sentence Parsing: Empirical Evidence, Computational Modelling, and Simulations
papers.research_question: How does memory retrieval work during online sentence parsing, and under what conditions does similarity-based interference occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model, which successfully predicts similarity-based interference data in floating quantifier processing, emphasizing structural information and revision.
papers.conclusion: The RICB model accounts for the data and underscores the importance of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
Similarity-based interference was observed in ungrammatical sentences but not in grammatical sentences.
The interference patterns were not consistent with existing theories and models.
The RICB model, which assumes heavy weighting of structural cues and includes revision, predicts the observed data.
The results highlight the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during sentence processing.
papers.limitation:
Detecting similarity-based interference requires large sample sizes, particularly in grammatical sentences.
The patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models.
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper reports two experiments (Experiments 1 and 2) and computational simulations designed to investigate and model memory retrieval processes during real-time sentence processing. Central to this study is the hypothesis that linguistic information serves as a cue to retrieve target representations from memory during dependency formation. The basis for this cue-based memory retrieval stems from research showing that non-target representations that match a set of retrieval cues interfere with target retrieval. The susceptibility to this similarity-based interference has been debated in the sentence processing literature, and various hypotheses and models have been formulated and developed. This issue is addressed empirically in Experiments 1 and 2, which investigated similarity-based interference in sentences with a floating quantifier. Bayesian linear mixed models and Bayes factor analyses suggested similarity-based interference. However, the patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models. To reconcile these findings within the framework of cue-based memory retrieval, this paper implements the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model based on the ACT–R architecture. This model assumes that structural information is heavily weighted and incorporates the notions of initial retrieval and revision. The results of the simulations indicate that the RICB model successfully predicts the observed data, highlighting the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: To Copy or Not to Copy: Copying Is Easier to Induce Than Recall
papers.research_question: Can the model’s choice of information be controlled by a targeted intervention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an arbitration vector that isolates the control signal for choosing between parametric recall and contextual copying, and shows that injecting this vector can steer model behavior, with copying being easier to induce than recall.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that copying from context is easier to induce than recalling from parametric knowledge, revealing an asymmetry in the model's arbitration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
The arbitration vector extracted from residual stream centroids can steer behavior between Copy→Recall and Recall→Copy.
Copying is easier to induce than recall: Recall→Copy requires smaller scaling and works from multiple token positions, while Copy→Recall requires larger scaling and only works at the object token.
The steering effect is spatially localized: effective layers differ for the two directions.
The intervention causes changes in attention routing and MLP contributions, with successful jamming of attention to the context only when applied at the object token.
The model's fluency (perplexity) is maintained at moderate scaling but degrades at extreme scaling.
papers.abstract: Language models used in retrieval-augmented settings must arbitrate between parametric knowledge stored in their weights and contextual information in the prompt. This work presents a mechanistic study of that choice by extracting an \emph{arbitration vector} from model activations on a curated dataset designed to disentangle (i) irrelevant contexts that elicit parametric recall and (ii) relevant but false contexts that elicit copying. The vector is computed as the residual-stream centroid difference between these regimes across 27 relations, and is injected as an additive intervention at selected layers and token spans to steer behavior in two directions: Copy$\rightarrow$Recall (suppressing context use) and Recall$\rightarrow$Copy (inducing the model to copy any token from the context). Experiments on two architectures (decoder-only and encoder/decoder) and two open-domain QA benchmarks show consistent behavior shifts under moderate scaling while monitoring accuracy and fluency. Mechanistic analyses of attention routing, MLP contributions, and layer-wise probability trajectories reveal an asymmetry: inducing copying is an easy ``reactivation'' process that can be triggered at different locations in the input, while restoring recall is a ``suppression'' process that is more fragile and strongly tied to object-token interventions.

papers.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
papers.research_question: How do long-context language models retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the input?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and characterizes 'retrieval heads', a sparse set of attention heads responsible for retrieving information from long contexts, and shows they are universal, intrinsic, and causally important for factuality and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval heads implement a conditional copy algorithm and are the primary reason why long-context models can pass the Needle-in-a-Haystack test; their activation explains model factuality versus hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are universal and sparse, existing in all tested long-context models and constituting less than 5% of attention heads.
Retrieval heads are intrinsic, already present in base models and reused in derived models (e.g., via continued pretraining or fine-tuning).
Retrieval heads are dynamically activated based on the specific tokens and context required for retrieval.
Retrieval heads are causal; pruning them leads to retrieval failure and hallucination, while pruning non-retrieval heads does not.
Retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought reasoning tasks, which require frequent reference to input information, but have less impact on tasks relying on internal knowledge.
future_direction: Fostering future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
Discovering more algorithm and functionalities implemented by other types of attention heads.
Applying insights to KV cache compression by pruning non-retrieval head caches.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress in long-context language models, it remains elusive how transformer-based models exhibit the capability to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context. This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across a wide spectrum of models reveals that a special type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving information, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify intriguing properties of retrieval heads:(1) universal: all the explored models with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small portion (less than 5\%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending the context length by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random non-retrieval heads does not affect the model's retrieval ability. We further show that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context. Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the input tokens. We believe our insights will foster future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.

papers.title: Beyond Semantics: How Temporal Biases Shape Retrieval in Transformer and State-Space Models
papers.research_question: How do temporal biases shape information retrieval in transformer and state-space models during in-context learning, and how effectively can these models differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that both transformer and state-space models exhibit strong temporal biases (primacy and recency effects) in retrieving information, and in transformers, these biases are mechanistically linked to the function of induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Temporal biases are fundamental to in-context learning in both transformer and state-space architectures, shaping information retrieval in ways analogous to human episodic memory, with induction heads playing a key mechanistic role in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Both transformer and state-space models show a tendency for serial recall, predicting the token immediately following a repeated instance ('+1' token).
The strength of serial recall is modulated by the token's temporal position, showing strong primacy and recency effects, with model-specific biases (e.g., Mistral shows recency, Falcon-Mamba shows primacy).
Ablating induction heads in transformers significantly impairs both serial recall and the ability to selectively retrieve correct episodes in the presence of interference, confirming their causal role.
Despite architectural differences, state-space models exhibit comparable temporal biases to transformers, suggesting these biases arise from fundamental properties of sequential data processing.
Episodic retrieval is less reliable for memories embedded in the middle of a prompt, demonstrating a 'lost in the middle' effect even when semantic content is neutralized.
papers.limitation: The study primarily uses token-random prompts rather than natural text and analyzes next-token probabilities, representing a simplified information environment that isolates temporal effects from semantic confounds.
future_direction: Future work can explore the more complex interplay between 'when' something was said and 'what' was said in rich, semantic contexts.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is governed by both temporal and semantic relationships, shaping how Large Language Models (LLMs) retrieve contextual information. Analogous to human episodic memory, where the retrieval of specific events is enabled by separating events that happened at different times, this work probes the ability of various pretrained LLMs, including transformer and state-space models, to differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events. Specifically, we prompted models with sequences containing multiple presentations of the same token, which reappears at the sequence end. By fixing the positions of these repeated tokens and permuting all others, we removed semantic confounds and isolated temporal effects on next-token prediction. Across diverse sequences, models consistently placed the highest probabilities on tokens following a repeated token, but with a notable bias for those nearest the beginning or end of the input. An ablation experiment linked this phenomenon in transformers to induction heads. Extending the analysis to unique semantic contexts with partial overlap further demonstrated that memories embedded in the middle of a prompt are retrieved less reliably. Despite architectural differences, state-space and transformer models showed comparable temporal biases. Our findings deepen the understanding of temporal biases in in-context learning and offer an illustration of how these biases can enable temporal separation and episodic retrieval.

papers.title: How Retrieved Context Shapes Internal Representations in RAG
papers.research_question: How do different types of retrieved documents influence the internal representations that govern generation in RAG?
papers.core_contribution: This paper studies RAG from a representation-level perspective, analyzing how LLMs internally process retrieved context. It finds that random documents induce large representation drift associated with abstention, relevant documents preserve representations and act as confirmation signals, and a single relevant document stabilizes representations in multi-document settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a representation-level perspective on RAG, complementing prior output-focused analyses. It offers mechanistic explanations for phenomena such as the distracting effect and confirmation bias, and insights for designing more reliable RAG systems.
papers.key_findings:
Random documents induce large representation drift, which is linked to abstention behavior in instruction-tuned models.
Relevant documents largely preserve internal representations, acting primarily as confirmation signals rather than introducing decisive new information.
In multi-document settings, a single relevant document anchors internal representations and suppresses the influence of additional distracting or random documents.
LLMs distinguish prompts with random documents from others in early layers, but separating relevant from distracting documents requires deeper processing and remains imperfect.
Later layers increasingly emphasize parametric knowledge, closing the gap between no-document and relevant-document representations and limiting the influence of retrieved evidence on hard queries.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses primarily on the last prompt token representations and their evolution across layers, which does not capture token-level dynamics within the context or during response generation.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by conditioning generation on retrieved external documents, but the effect of retrieved context is often non-trivial. In realistic retrieval settings, the retrieved document set often contains a mixture of documents that vary in relevance and usefulness. While prior work has largely examined these phenomena through output behavior, little is known about how retrieved context shapes the internal representations that mediate information integration in RAG. In this work, we study RAG through the lens of latent representations. We systematically analyze how different types of retrieved documents affect the hidden states of LLMs, and how these internal representation shifts relate to downstream generation behavior. Across four question-answering datasets and three LLMs, we analyze internal representations under controlled single- and multi-document settings. Our results reveal how context relevancy and layer-wise processing influence internal representations, providing explanations on LLMs output behaviors and insights for RAG system design.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Llama See, Llama Do: A Mechanistic Perspective on Contextual Entrainment and Distraction in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do language models become distracted by irrelevant contextual information, and what is the mechanistic basis for this distraction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies contextual entrainment, a novel phenomenon where LMs assign higher probabilities to tokens that appear in the context, and discovers entrainment heads that control this effect, providing a mechanistic perspective on distraction.
papers.conclusion: Contextual entrainment is a novel mechanistic phenomenon that plays a crucial role in LM distraction, and interpretability techniques can provide insights for real-world applications such as RAG.
papers.key_findings:
LMs assign significantly higher logits/probabilities to tokens that have appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens (contextual entrainment).
The magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors, with counterfactual prompts having a stronger effect than factual ones.
A small set of attention heads (entrainment heads) are responsible for contextual entrainment; disabling them attenuates the effect.
Entrainment heads are relation-specific, not model-specific.
Removing entrainment heads has minimal impact on other LM capabilities like factual recall and in-context learning.
papers.limitation:
Did not conduct experiments using larger LMs due to resource limitations.
Only used the LRE dataset and not standard RAG datasets.
Do not propose an application to mitigate the distraction problem.
future_direction: Reproduce results using larger models.
Validate findings using standard RAG datasets.
Further steps toward addressing the distraction problem.
papers.abstract: We observe a novel phenomenon, contextual entrainment, across a wide range of language models (LMs) and prompt settings, providing a new mechanistic perspective on how LMs become distracted by ``irrelevant'' contextual information in the input prompt. Specifically, LMs assign significantly higher logits (or probabilities) to any tokens that have previously appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens. This suggests that contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, occurring independently of the relevance or semantic relation of the tokens to the question or the rest of the sentence. We find statistically significant evidence that the magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors. Counterfactual prompts have a greater effect compared to factual ones, suggesting that while contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, it is modulated by semantic factors. We hypothesise that there is a circuit of attention heads -- the entrainment heads -- that corresponds to the contextual entrainment phenomenon. Using a novel entrainment head discovery method based on differentiable masking, we identify these heads across various settings. When we ``turn off'' these heads, i.e., set their outputs to zero, the effect of contextual entrainment is significantly attenuated, causing the model to generate output that capitulates to what it would produce if no distracting context were provided. Our discovery of contextual entrainment, along with our investigation into LM distraction via the entrainment heads, marks a key step towards the mechanistic analysis and mitigation of the distraction problem.

papers.title: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories
papers.research_question: How do transformers store factual information and what is their storage capacity?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow transformers can achieve near-optimal storage capacity for factual recall by using associative memories in both self-attention and MLP components, with a trade-off between them.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently store factual information using associative memories implemented in self-attention and MLP components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear and MLP associative memories can store a number of associations proportional to their parameter count.
A one-layer transformer can achieve 100% accuracy on a synthetic factual recall task when either the total self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scale linearly with the number of facts.
The transformer exhibits sequential learning dynamics during training, with an initial 'hallucination' stage.
The storage constructions are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
papers.limitation: The linear associative memory construction requires the association function to be injective for optimal capacity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated an impressive ability to perform factual recall. Prior work has found that transformers trained on factual recall tasks can store information at a rate proportional to their parameter count. In our work, we show that shallow transformers can use a combination of associative memories to obtain such near optimal storage capacity. We begin by proving that the storage capacities of both linear and MLP associative memories scale linearly with parameter count. We next introduce a synthetic factual recall task, and prove that a transformer with a single layer of self-attention followed by an MLP can obtain 100% accuracy on the task whenever either the total number of self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scales (up to log factors) linearly with the number of facts. In particular, the transformer can trade off between using the value matrices or the MLP as an associative memory to store the dataset of facts. We complement these expressivity results with an analysis of the gradient flow trajectory of a simplified linear attention model trained on our factual recall task, where we show that the model exhibits sequential learning behavior.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Locating and Extracting Relational Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are relational concepts represented within large language models, and can they be located and extracted?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that hidden states in shallow layers at the last token position solely express relational concepts, and demonstrates that these relational representations can be extracted and used for zero-shot relational reasoning and controllable fact recall via relation rewriting.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that relational representations can be located and extracted from LLMs, are faithful and robust, and can be used to control model responses, providing a stepping stone towards understanding the internal knowledge system of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden states at the last token position in shallow layers (the 'Relational Emergence stage') exclusively manifest the causal effects of relations, without subject information.
These relational representations can be accurately located and transplanted to other fact-recall processes, enabling the recall of new objects.
Extracted relational representations are faithful and robust entity connectors, enabling zero-shot relational reasoning with accuracy comparable to full-prompt prompting.
Relational representations can be used for controllable fact recall via 'relation rewriting', guiding model outputs to align with a desired relation without parameter modification.
The three-stage observation (Initial, Relational Emergence, Conjoint Influence) for locating relational representations does not hold for linguistic tasks (e.g., past tense prediction), limiting the method's applicability.
papers.limitation: The three-stage observation for locating relational representations is uncommon in fact recall processes involving linguistics (e.g., predicting past tense), where subject causal effects emerge before relations, limiting the method to non-linguistic relation location and extraction.
future_direction: Future research on how attention allocation is related to the causal effects of subjects and relations.
papers.abstract: Relational concepts are indeed foundational to the structure of knowledge representation, as they facilitate the association between various entity concepts, allowing us to express and comprehend complex world knowledge. By expressing relational concepts in natural language prompts, people can effortlessly interact with large language models (LLMs) and recall desired factual knowledge. However, the process of knowledge recall lacks interpretability, and representations of relational concepts within LLMs remain unknown to us. In this paper, we identify hidden states that can express entity and relational concepts through causal mediation analysis in fact recall processes. Our finding reveals that at the last token position of the input prompt, there are hidden states that solely express the causal effects of relational concepts. Based on this finding, we assume that these hidden states can be treated as relational representations and we can successfully extract them from LLMs. The experimental results demonstrate high credibility of the relational representations: they can be flexibly transplanted into other fact recall processes, and can also be used as robust entity connectors. Moreover, we also show that the relational representations exhibit significant potential for controllable fact recall through relation rewriting.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle
papers.research_question: How do attention layers in transformer-based LLMs implement memory retrieval mechanisms, and are contextual cues represented as keywords?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval, with Q, K, V playing distinct roles analogous to human memory, and that contextual cues are represented as keywords.
papers.conclusion: Attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval mechanisms guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, with keywords serving as retrieval cues and specific neurons encoding these cues.
papers.key_findings:
Swapping V alone induces hallucinations, indicating V stores content.
Swapping both K and V induces systematic hallucination, showing content-addressable matching and content retrieval.
Swapping K only hinders factual recall, representing retrieval failure.
Consistent, model-specific attention neurons are activated by keywords.
Perturbing keywords at the K matrix impairs memory retrieval.
papers.abstract: While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for large language models (LLMs) remains an evolving field with many unresolved questions, increasing regulatory pressures have spurred interest in its role in ensuring transparency, accountability, and privacy-preserving machine unlearning. Despite recent advances in XAI have provided some insights, the specific role of attention layers in transformer based LLMs remains underexplored. This study investigates the memory mechanisms instantiated by attention layers, drawing on prior research in psychology and computational psycholinguistics that links Transformer attention to cue based retrieval in human memory. In this view, queries encode the retrieval context, keys index candidate memory traces, attention weights quantify cue trace similarity, and values carry the encoded content, jointly enabling the construction of a context representation that precedes and facilitates memory retrieval. Guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, we hypothesize that the cues used in the initial stage of retrieval are instantiated as keywords. We provide converging evidence for this keywords-as-cues hypothesis. In addition, we isolate neurons within attention layers whose activations selectively encode and facilitate the retrieval of context-defining keywords. Consequently, these keywords can be extracted from identified neurons and further contribute to downstream applications such as unlearning.

papers.title: Quantifying reliance on external information over parametric knowledge during Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) using mechanistic analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models balance the use of external retrieved context versus internal parametric knowledge during Retrieval Augmented Generation, and do they exhibit a bias towards external information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models in RAG settings exhibit a strong bias towards using external retrieved context over internal parametric knowledge, demonstrating a 'shortcut' effect through mechanistic analysis.
papers.conclusion: Using three mechanistic probing techniques, we observe reduced reliance on parametric memory, reduced information flow from the subject token to the last token residual stream, and a shortcut behavior where information from the attribute token flows to the last token residual stream during factual predictions in the RAG setting.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals a ~10X decrease in Average Indirect Effect for LLaMa-2 and ~35X for Phi-2 on the last subject token in RAG setting, indicating reduced use of parametric memory.
Attention contributions from subject token to last token decrease by ~1.6X for LLaMa-2 and 7X for Phi-2 in RAG compared to non-RAG.
Attention knockouts on subject token lead to less than 5% drop in answer probabilities in RAG, compared to 20-25% in non-RAG, showing reduced dependence on subject token.
The last token residual stream is enriched from RAG-context tokens rather than subject tokens in RAG setting.
papers.limitation:
Study limited to smaller models (up to 7B parameters), not larger LMs.
Context generated synthetically using GPT-4, not from a conventional RAG pipeline.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger language models (>13B parameters).
Study impact of context length and primacy/recency bias.
Replicate findings using conventional RAG pipeline instead of synthetic GPT-4 context.
papers.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a widely used approach for leveraging external context in several natural language applications such as question answering and information retrieval. Yet, the exact nature in which a Language Model (LM) leverages this non-parametric memory or retrieved context isn't clearly understood. This paper mechanistically examines the RAG pipeline to highlight that LMs demonstrate a "shortcut'' effect and have a strong bias towards utilizing the retrieved context to answer questions, while relying minimally on model priors. We propose (a) Causal Mediation Analysis; for proving that parametric memory is minimally utilized when answering a question and (b) Attention Contributions and Knockouts for showing the last token residual stream do not get enriched from the subject token in the question, but gets enriched from tokens of RAG-context. We find this pronounced "shortcut'' behaviour to be true across both LLMs (e.g.,LlaMa) and SLMs (e.g., Phi)

papers.title: Do LLMs "Feel"? Emotion Circuits Discovery and Control
papers.research_question: Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? What form do these mechanisms take? Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, enabling precise control of emotional expression without explicit prompting.
papers.conclusion: Emotion in LLMs arises from a structured hierarchy of neurons and attention heads whose coordinated activations form interpretable emotion circuits. The framework lays a foundation for extending circuit-level interpretability and controllable generation to broader cognitive and stylistic domains.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain context-agnostic emotion directions that are consistent across contexts.
Emotion expression is driven by a small set of neurons and attention heads that form interpretable circuits.
Modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy, outperforming prompting- and steering-based methods.
The emotion circuits are sparse and have low overlap across emotions for neurons and moderate overlap for attention heads.
The framework generalizes to different models (LLaMA and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Analyses are limited to English inputs.
The study focuses on Ekman’s six basic emotions, leaving richer affective spectra for future exploration.
The stability of the extracted circuits under fine-tuning or transfer learning remains to be explored.
future_direction: Verify whether similar emotion circuits emerge under multilingual contexts.
Explore richer affective spectra beyond the six basic emotions.
Explore the stability of the circuits under fine-tuning or transfer learning.
papers.abstract: As the demand for emotional intelligence in large language models (LLMs) grows, a key challenge lies in understanding the internal mechanisms that give rise to emotional expression and in controlling emotions in generated text. This study addresses three core questions: (1) Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? (2) What form do these mechanisms take? (3) Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control? We first construct a controlled dataset, SEV (Scenario-Event with Valence), to elicit comparable internal states across emotions. Subsequently, we extract context-agnostic emotion directions that reveal consistent, cross-context encoding of emotion (Q1). We identify neurons and attention heads that locally implement emotional computation through analytical decomposition and causal analysis, and validate their causal roles via ablation and enhancement interventions. Next, we quantify each sublayer's causal influence on the model's final emotion representation and integrate the identified local components into coherent global emotion circuits that drive emotional expression (Q2). Directly modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy on the test set, surpassing prompting- and steering-based methods (Q3). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, offering new insights into interpretability and controllable emotional intelligence.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Too Late to Recall: Explaining the Two-Hop Problem in Multimodal Knowledge Retrieval
papers.research_question: Why do many vision language models (VLMs) exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their large language model (LLM) backbones, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs suffer from a 'two-hop problem' where entity representations from visual inputs emerge too late in the forward pass, bypassing the early-layer MLP circuits in the LLM backbone responsible for factual recall, leading to performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms; representation misalignment limits VLMs' ability to reuse existing task circuits.
papers.key_findings:
