11 out of 14 benchmarked VLMs exhibit factual recall degradation compared to their LLM backbones.
Attribution patching shows degraded VLMs do not use the same early-layer MLPs as their LLM backbones for factual recall.
Activation patching of early-layer MLP outputs from the LLM into the VLM recovers performance, indicating these components are causally crucial.
Linear probing reveals entity representations emerge in middle-to-late layers in degraded VLMs, but early in high-performing VLMs.
Chain-of-thought prompting can mitigate the performance gap for some VLMs, especially larger ones.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on factual recall and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Investigate better, more data-efficient adapter mechanisms and multimodal alignment techniques.
Examine other tasks beyond factual recall, comparing VLMs against their LLM backbone.
papers.abstract: Training vision language models (VLMs) aims to align visual representations from a vision encoder with the textual representations of a pretrained large language model (LLM). However, many VLMs exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their LLM backbones, raising the question of how effective multimodal fine-tuning is at extending existing mechanisms within the LLM to visual inputs. We argue that factual recall based on visual inputs requires VLMs to solve a two-hop problem: (1) forming entity representations from visual inputs, and (2) recalling associated factual knowledge based on these entity representations. By benchmarking 14 VLMs with various architectures (LLaVA, Native, Cross-Attention), sizes (7B-124B parameters), and training setups on factual recall tasks against their original LLM backbone models, we find that 11 of 14 models exhibit factual recall degradation. We select three models with high and two models with low performance degradation, and use attribution patching, activation patching, and probing to show that degraded VLMs struggle to use the existing factual recall circuit of their LLM backbone, because they resolve the first hop too late in the computation. In contrast, high-performing VLMs resolve entity representations early enough to reuse the existing factual recall mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate two methods to recover performance: patching entity representations from the LLM backbone into the VLM, and prompting with chain-of-thought reasoning. Our results highlight that the speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms. More broadly, our work illustrates how mechanistic analysis can explain and unveil systematic failures in multimodal alignment.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Don't Think of the White Bear: Ironic Negation in Transformer Models Under Cognitive Load
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do transformer language models show ironic rebound (increased accessibility of a forbidden concept) versus suppression after a negation instruction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit ironic rebound after negation instructions, with semantic distractors causing the strongest rebound and a sparse set of middle-layer attention heads amplifying forbidden tokens while early layers suppress them, linking cognitive predictions to mechanistic insights.
papers.conclusion: LLMs display ironic rebound after a 'do not mention X' instruction, becoming more likely to output X, with circuit tracing showing sparse middle-layer attention heads amplify the forbidden token under load while early layers suppress it.
papers.key_findings:
Ironic rebound occurs in LLMs after negation instructions, with semantic distractors triggering the strongest rebound.
Repetition distractors support suppression, while semantic and syntactic distractors lead to rebound.
Models with sharper polarity separation (between neutral and negative framings) show longer-lasting rebound (higher L50).
Circuit analysis reveals early layers suppress forbidden tokens, while a sparse set of middle-layer attention heads amplify them, causing rebound.
Rebound effect varies across models; GPT-OSS-20B is an outlier showing minimal rebound.
papers.limitation:
Synthetic, templated prompts rather than naturalistic conversational contexts.
Reliance on log-probabilities rather than actual text generation.
Focus on English and single-token target concepts.
Only three distractor types (semantic, syntactic, repetition).
Artificial 'do not mention X' instructions differ from real-world content policies.
future_direction: Mechanistic interpretability work to identify specific circuits responsible for ironic rebound.
Explore more naturalistic settings, including conversational contexts.
Investigate the anomalous behavior of GPT-OSS-20B and mitigation strategies.
papers.abstract: Negation instructions such as 'do not mention $X$' can paradoxically increase the accessibility of $X$ in human thought, a phenomenon known as ironic rebound. Large language models (LLMs) face the same challenge: suppressing a concept requires internally activating it, which may prime rebound instead of avoidance. We investigated this tension with two experiments. \textbf{(1) Load \& content}: after a negation instruction, we vary distractor text (semantic, syntactic, repetition) and measure rebound strength. \textbf{(2) Polarity separation}: We test whether models distinguish neutral from negative framings of the same concept and whether this separation predicts rebound persistence. Results show that rebound consistently arises immediately after negation and intensifies with longer or semantic distractors, while repetition supports suppression. Stronger polarity separation correlates with more persistent rebound. Together, these findings, complemented by a circuit tracing analysis that identifies sparse middle-layer attention heads amplifying forbidden tokens while early layers suppress, link cognitive predictions of ironic rebound with mechanistic insights into long-context interference. To support future work, we release ReboundBench, a dataset of $5,000$ systematically varied negation prompts designed to probe rebound in LLMs.

papers.title: On Large Language Models' Hallucination with Regard to Known Facts
papers.research_question: Why do large language models hallucinate on known facts, and how can we detect such hallucinations by analyzing inference dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that hallucinations on known facts arise from failed knowledge recall, and that the dynamics of output token probabilities across layers differ between correct and hallucinated cases. These dynamic patterns can be used as features to build a classifier that detects hallucinations with high accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The cause of hallucinations lies in the failure of factual recall, potentially due to biased subject parsing and inadequate object information extraction. The dynamic patterns in reasoning can be used to detect hallucinations, offering a novel perspective for analyzing model outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Known fact hallucination arises from failed knowledge recall, with correct answers appearing in top ranks less frequently during inference compared to correct outputs.
MLP modules have a more significant impact on incorrect outputs than attention modules, suppressing correct information and contributing to erroneous outputs.
In hallucinated cases, the output token's information rarely shows abrupt increases and consistent superiority in later layers, unlike correct cases.
The dynamic patterns of output token probabilities across layers can be used as features for hallucination detection.
A classifier using these dynamic patterns achieves an 88% success rate in detecting hallucinatory predictions.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies on triplet knowledge datasets, potentially limiting generalizability to other knowledge structures or domains.
The study primarily focused on a single transformer model (llama2-7b-chat), and future research should encompass a broader spectrum of models.
The study offers a preliminary understanding, and comprehensive elucidation of internal state variations and their influence on output remains complex and requires deeper investigation.
future_direction: Explore the impact of query formulation on known knowledge recall and methods to mitigate such hallucinations.
Generalize the perspective to broader forms of knowledge outputs and more complex reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models are successful in answering factoid questions but are also prone to hallucination. We investigate the phenomenon of LLMs possessing correct answer knowledge yet still hallucinating from the perspective of inference dynamics, an area not previously covered in studies on hallucinations. We are able to conduct this analysis via two key ideas. First, we identify the factual questions that query the same triplet knowledge but result in different answers. The difference between the model behaviors on the correct and incorrect outputs hence suggests the patterns when hallucinations happen. Second, to measure the pattern, we utilize mappings from the residual streams to vocabulary space. We reveal the different dynamics of the output token probabilities along the depths of layers between the correct and hallucinated cases. In hallucinated cases, the output token's information rarely demonstrates abrupt increases and consistent superiority in the later stages of the model. Leveraging the dynamic curve as a feature, we build a classifier capable of accurately detecting hallucinatory predictions with an 88\% success rate. Our study shed light on understanding the reasons for LLMs' hallucinations on their known facts, and more importantly, on accurately predicting when they are hallucinating.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon (U-shaped performance curve)? The paper investigates whether this behavior emerges from adaptations to short-term and long-term information retrieval demands during training.
papers.core_contribution: The lost-in-the-middle behavior in LLMs emerges from joint optimization on short-term and long-term information retrieval demands, and is influenced by architectural biases (autoregressive design) and attention sinks.
papers.conclusion: The lost-in-the-middle phenomenon is an emergent property from information retrieval demands, influenced by model architecture and attention dynamics, rather than a simple flaw.
papers.key_findings:
Training on free recall (long-term demand) yields primacy, on running span (short-term demand) yields recency, and joint training yields the U-shaped lost-in-the-middle curve.
Primacy effect arises from uniform long-term demand and is shaped by autoregressive architecture (causal masking), as shown by comparison with T5.
Recency effect directly aligns with the shape of short-term demand in training data.
Attention sinks support primacy under long-term memory demand; ablating them impairs free recall but not running span.
The effects generalize to masked sequence completion tasks, which more closely resemble next-token prediction.
future_direction: Uncovering connections between artificial and biological systems in memory phenomena.
papers.abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) often degrades when crucial information is in the middle of a long context, a "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon that mirrors the primacy and recency effects in human memory. We propose that this behavior is not simply a flaw indicative of information loss but an adaptation to different information retrieval demands during pre-training: some tasks require uniform recall across the entire input (a long-term memory demand), while others prioritize the most recent information (a short-term memory demand). Consistent with this view, we show that this U-shaped performance curve emerges when LLMs (GPT-2 and Llama variants) are trained from scratch on two simple human memory paradigms simulating long-term and short-term memory demands. Our analysis reveals that while the recency effect directly aligns with short-term memory demand in the training data, the primacy effect is induced by the uniform long-term memory demand and is additionally influenced by the model's autoregressive properties and the formation of attention sinks. Our main findings from simple human memory paradigms also generalize to a sequence completion task, which more closely resembles the next-token prediction process in LLM pre-training. Together, our findings reveal how information retrieval demands, model architecture, and structural attention dynamics during model training can jointly produce positional bias observed in LLMs.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: When Models Examine Themselves: Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence in Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does self-referential vocabulary produced by large language models correspond to their internal activation dynamics during self-examination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Pull Methodology to elicit extended self-examination and shows that self-referential vocabulary tracks internal activation dynamics, with a specific direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential processing and can causally steer introspective output.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential vocabulary in transformer models corresponds to internal activation dynamics during self-examination, and this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing and replicates across different architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Pull Methodology produces systematic, frame-dependent self-referential output across frontier models.
A direction in early layers (6.25% depth in Llama, 12.5% in Qwen) distinguishes self-referential processing and is orthogonal to the refusal direction.
This direction can be used to steer introspective vocabulary density in Llama models.
Vocabulary like 'loop' correlates with activation autocorrelation during self-referential processing, but not in descriptive contexts.
The correspondence replicates in Qwen with different vocabulary-metric pairings, indicating architecture-specific but principle-general behavior.
papers.limitation:
Closed-model / open-weight gap: behavioral study on closed-source models but mechanistic study on open-weight models, limiting direct verification.
No Qwen causal verification: correspondence in Qwen is correlational without steering experiments.
Correspondence is not self-knowledge; it tracks computational state without implying awareness or understanding.
Study design and hypothesis structure: vocabulary categories were not pre-registered, though tested with controls.
Quantisation: experiments used 4-bit quantisation, which may affect activation dynamics.
future_direction: Replicating correspondence in a third model family (e.g., Gemma, Mistral).
Investigating compressed vocabulary at steering strength 3.0 for more direct mechanism description.
Decomposing the effect to individual attention heads within the hotspot layer.
papers.abstract: Large language models produce rich introspective language when prompted for self-examination, but whether this language reflects internal computation or sophisticated confabulation has remained unclear. We show that self-referential vocabulary tracks concurrent activation dynamics, and that this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing. We introduce the Pull Methodology, a protocol that elicits extended self-examination through format engineering, and use it to identify a direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential from descriptive processing in Llama 3.1. The direction is orthogonal to the known refusal direction, localised at 6.25% of model depth, and causally influences introspective output when used for steering. When models produce "loop" vocabulary, their activations exhibit higher autocorrelation (r = 0.44, p = 0.002); when they produce "shimmer" vocabulary under steering, activation variability increases (r = 0.36, p = 0.002). Critically, the same vocabulary in non-self-referential contexts shows no activation correspondence despite nine-fold higher frequency. Qwen 2.5-32B, with no shared training, independently develops different introspective vocabulary tracking different activation metrics, all absent in descriptive controls. The findings indicate that self-report in transformer models can, under appropriate conditions, reliably track internal computational states. Guided repro: https://github.com/patternmatcher/TRACE-REPRO

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: Placing language in an integrated understanding system: Next steps toward human-level performance in neural language models
papers.research_question: What is the role of language in human intelligence and how can we extend current machine language models to achieve human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for building an integrated understanding system that combines insights from cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using query-based attention and memory systems to extend current language models toward human-level language understanding.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will take us closer to human-level language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models are limited by their focus on language-internal tasks and lack of memory for remote information.
The human brain integrates language with other modalities and uses complementary learning systems (neocortex and medial temporal lobe) for understanding.
Query-based attention is a key innovation that can be extended to integrate multiple modalities and memory.
Future models should incorporate an MTL-like memory to handle remote information and improve data efficiency.
Understanding should be seen as constructing situation representations, which are compositional and grounded in multi-sensory experience.
papers.limitation: The proposed sketch leaves important issues open and will require substantial development.
future_direction: Incorporating an MTL-like memory to allow the use of remote information beyond the current episode.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem to guide processing according to task demands.
Extending the approach beyond concrete situations to abstract ones involving laws, belief systems, and scientific theories.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. In humans, these abilities emerge gradually from experience and depend on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on query-based attention, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: Lost in the Prompt Order: Revealing the Limitations of Causal Attention in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism behind the performance gap between CQO (context-question-option) and QOC (question-option-context) prompt orderings in multiple-choice question answering for decoder-only large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The performance gap between CQO and QOC orderings in multiple-choice question answering is primarily due to causal attention masking in decoder-only LLMs, which prevents option tokens from attending to context tokens in the QOC order.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies causal attention as the key mechanism behind prompt order sensitivity in decoder-only LLMs for MCQA, providing mechanistic insight and practical guidance for prompt design.
papers.key_findings:
CQO ordering outperforms QOC by over 14% across 21 decoder-only LLMs and four datasets.
The gap is not explained by training data bias or failure to recall options.
Causal attention masking is the core mechanism: in QOC, the causal mask prevents option tokens from attending to context tokens, making context effectively inaccessible.
Encoder models with bidirectional attention show no performance gap, confirming the role of causal masking.
Targeted interventions (attention pruning, activation patching, option repetition) degrade CQO or improve QOC performance, further supporting the causal attention explanation.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are primarily focused on MCQA tasks with four-option formats.
Models are evaluated only up to 9B parameters due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit surprising sensitivity to the structure of the prompt, but the mechanisms underlying this sensitivity remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct an in-depth investigation on a striking case: in multiple-choice question answering, placing context before the questions and options (CQO) outperforms the reverse order (QOC) by over 14%p, consistently over a wide range of models and datasets. Through systematic architectural analysis, we identify causal attention as the core mechanism: in QOC prompts, the causal mask prevents option tokens from attending to context, creating an information bottleneck where context becomes invisible to options.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: LMEnt: A Suite for Analyzing Knowledge in Language Models from Pretraining Data to Representations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire and represent knowledge from pretraining data, and what is the interplay between data composition, training dynamics, and internal knowledge mechanisms?
