papers.core_contribution: Introduces LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in language models, including annotated pretraining data, entity-based retrieval, and pretrained models, enabling studies on the connection between data and knowledge representations.
papers.conclusion: LMEnt provides a flexible testbed for investigating knowledge representations in language models and facilitates future research on knowledge acquisition and editing.
papers.key_findings:
LMEnt's entity-based retrieval outperforms string-based methods by up to 80.4% in returning relevant document chunks.
LMEnt models achieve comparable knowledge recall performance to models trained on orders of magnitude more data.
Knowledge acquisition is correlated with fact frequency, but both learning and forgetting rates increase with frequency.
Increasing model size improves learning of frequent facts but has little effect on tail facts.
papers.limitation:
Pretraining data is relatively small and models are compute-efficient, which may limit generalizability.
Does not compare with dense retrievers like DPR or ColBERT.
Focuses only on pretraining, not mid- or post-training phases.
future_direction: Investigating knowledge plasticity and editing during pretraining.
Improving factuality of LMs using entity annotations.
Extending LMEnt to other data sources and architectures.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) increasingly drive real-world applications that require world knowledge. However, the internal processes through which models turn data into representations of knowledge and beliefs about the world, are poorly understood. Insights into these processes could pave the way for developing LMs with knowledge representations that are more consistent, robust, and complete. To facilitate studying these questions, we present LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in LMs during pretraining. LMEnt introduces: (1) a knowledge-rich pretraining corpus, fully annotated with entity mentions, based on Wikipedia, (2) an entity-based retrieval method over pretraining data that outperforms previous approaches by as much as 80.4%, and (3) 12 pretrained models with up to 1B parameters and 4K intermediate checkpoints, with comparable performance to popular open-sourced models on knowledge benchmarks. Together, these resources provide a controlled environment for analyzing connections between entity mentions in pretraining and downstream performance, and the effects of causal interventions in pretraining data. We show the utility of LMEnt by studying knowledge acquisition across checkpoints, finding that fact frequency is key, but does not fully explain learning trends. We release LMEnt to support studies of knowledge in LMs, including knowledge representations, plasticity, editing, attribution, and learning dynamics.

papers.title: Delving into the Reversal Curse: How Far Can Large Language Models Generalize?
papers.research_question: How does the reversal curse manifest across various tasks, and what are the underlying generalization abilities and problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the reversal curse is more likely a backward recall deficiency, and identifies an inherent 'thinking bias' in LLMs where they preferentially use names to initiate fact recall, which strongly influences their generalization ability based on training data structure.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse is a backward recall deficiency in decoder-only models, and LLMs' inherent thinking bias underscores the critical importance of appropriate training data structure for successful knowledge application and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can generalize to 'B is A' when both A and B are presented in context (e.g., in multiple-choice questions).
Generalization ability is highly correlated with the structure of training documents (works for '[Name] is [Description]' but not the reverse).
LLMs possess an inherent thinking bias: they consistently start fact recall with names provided in the query.
The negative impact of this bias on downstream task performance is hard to mitigate through training alone.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) showcase unprecedented capabilities, they also exhibit certain inherent limitations when facing seemingly trivial tasks. A prime example is the recently debated "reversal curse", which surfaces when models, having been trained on the fact "A is B", struggle to generalize this knowledge to infer that "B is A". In this paper, we examine the manifestation of the reversal curse across various tasks and delve into both the generalization abilities and the problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs. This investigation leads to a series of significant insights: (1) LLMs are able to generalize to "B is A" when both A and B are presented in the context as in the case of a multiple-choice question. (2) This generalization ability is highly correlated to the structure of the fact "A is B" in the training documents. For example, this generalization only applies to biographies structured in "[Name] is [Description]" but not to "[Description] is [Name]". (3) We propose and verify the hypothesis that LLMs possess an inherent bias in fact recalling during knowledge application, which explains and underscores the importance of the document structure to successful learning. (4) The negative impact of this bias on the downstream performance of LLMs can hardly be mitigated through training alone. These findings offer a novel perspective on interpreting LLMs' generalization through their intrinsic mechanisms and provide insights for developing more effective learning methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alibaba/thinking_bias.git.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence.
Memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network.
The first layer is especially critical for memorized predictions.
The findings generalize from idioms to factual statements.
The IDIO MEM dataset is constructed for probing memorization and released for the community.
papers.abstract: To produce accurate predictions, language models (LMs) must balance between generalization and memorization. Yet, little is known about the mechanism by which transformer LMs employ their memorization capacity. When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory? In this work, we offer the first methodological framework for probing and characterizing recall of memorized sequences in transformer LMs. First, we lay out criteria for detecting model inputs that trigger memory recall, and propose idioms as inputs that typically fulfill these criteria. Next, we construct a dataset of English idioms and use it to compare model behavior on memorized vs. non-memorized inputs. Specifically, we analyze the internal prediction construction process by interpreting the model's hidden representations as a gradual refinement of the output probability distribution. We find that across different model sizes and architectures, memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence. This suggests that memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network. Last, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology beyond idioms in memorized factual statements. Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations. To explore this question, we build on previous work showing that LLM representations encode statement truthfulness -- i.e., true, factual statements can be easily separated from false, inaccurate ones. Specifically, we test the robustness of learned knowledge by evaluating representation separability on samples that have undergone superficial transformations to drive them out-of-distribution (OOD), such as typos or reformulations. By applying semantically-preserving perturbations, we study how separability degrades as statements become more OOD, across four LLM families, five evaluation datasets, and three knowledge probing methods. Our results reveal that internal representations of statement truthfulness collapse as the samples' presentations become less similar to those seen during pre-training. While LLMs can often distinguish between true and false statements when they closely resemble the pre-training data, this ability is highly dependent on the statement's exact surface form. These findings offer a possible explanation for brittle benchmark performance: LLMs may learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that allow for only limited generalizability. Our work presents a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes, and more broadly, calls for further research on improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Correspondence between the layered structure of deep language models and temporal structure of natural language processing in the human brain
papers.research_question: Does the layered hierarchy of deep language models (DLMs) correspond to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain? Specifically, is there a correlation between DLM layer depth and the time at which layers are most predictive of human brain activity?
papers.core_contribution: The layered hierarchy of deep language models (specifically GPT2-XL) corresponds to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain, with early layers predicting early neural responses and later layers predicting later responses in high-order language areas.
papers.conclusion: The internal sequence of computations across layers in deep language models models the temporal hierarchy of language comprehension in the human brain, providing evidence for shared computational principles between DLMs and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong positive correlation (Pearson r=0.85 in IFG) between DLM layer depth and the time of peak encoding performance in high-order language areas (IFG, TP, aSTG).
Intermediate layers of GPT2-XL (e.g., layer 22 in IFG) provide the best overall prediction of neural activity across language areas, forming an inverted U-shaped curve.
For predictable words, the temporal sequence is clear; for unpredictable words, the pattern is weaker and early layers shift to later lags (around 300ms) in IFG.
The temporal progression timescale increases along the ventral linguistic hierarchy, with the largest within-ROI temporal separation in the Temporal Pole (over 500 ms).
The observed lag-layer correlation is due to nonlinear transformations in the DLM, as linear interpolations between first and last layer embeddings yield significantly lower correlations.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a single DLM (GPT2-XL) and a single narrative stimulus, limiting generalizability.
The temporal resolution of the ECoG measurements, although high, was binned at 50 ms, which may not disambiguate layers that peak at similar times.
The hierarchical structure of DLMs is spatial, while that of the brain is spatiotemporal, representing a fundamental architectural difference.
future_direction: Explore other model architectures (e.g., recurrent, convolutional, or models with explicit temporal dynamics) to see if they better capture brain dynamics.
Use longer contexts and more diverse stimuli to test the robustness of the layer-time correspondence.
Investigate how DLMs might be augmented (e.g., with recurrence or explicit temporal hierarchies) to better model the brain's spatiotemporal language processing.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep language models (DLMs) provide a novel computational paradigm for how the brain processes natural language. Unlike symbolic, rule-based models described in psycholinguistics, DLMs encode words and their context as continuous numerical vectors. These “embeddings” are constructed by a sequence of computations organized in “layers” to ultimately capture surprisingly sophisticated representations of linguistic structures. How does this layered hierarchy map onto the human brain during natural language comprehension? In this study, we used electrocorticography (ECoG) to record neural activity in language areas along the superior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus while human participants listened to a 30-minute spoken narrative. We supplied this same narrative to a high-performing DLM (GPT2-XL) and extracted the contextual embeddings for each word in the story across all 48 layers of the model. We next trained a set of linear encoding models to predict the temporally-evolving neural activity from the embeddings at each layer. We found a striking correspondence between the layer-by-layer sequence of embeddings from GPT2-XL and the temporal sequence of neural activity in language areas. In addition, we found evidence for the gradual accumulation of recurrent information along the linguistic processing hierarchy. However, we also noticed additional neural processes in the brain, but not in DLMs, during the processing of surprising (unpredictable) words. These findings point to a connection between human language processing and DLMs where the layer-by-layer accumulation of contextual information in DLM embeddings matches the temporal dynamics of neural activity in high-order language areas.

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Massive Values in Self-Attention Modules are the Key to Contextual Knowledge Understanding
papers.research_question: What is the role of massive values in self-attention queries and keys, and how do they contribute to contextual knowledge understanding versus parametric knowledge retrieval?
papers.core_contribution: Massive values in attention queries and keys are critical for contextual knowledge understanding, and their concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE).
papers.conclusion: The findings shed new light on how queries and keys operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Massive values are concentrated in specific regions of attention queries and keys exclusively in models with RoPE.
These massive values are critical for contextual knowledge understanding rather than parametric knowledge retrieval.
Quantization methods that protect massive values preserve contextual understanding capabilities.
The concentration of massive values is caused by RoPE and appears from the first layers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in contextual knowledge understanding. In this paper, we show that these concentrated massive values consistently emerge in specific regions of attention queries (Q) and keys (K) while not having such patterns in values (V) in various modern transformer-based LLMs (Q, K, and V mean the representations output by the query, key, and value layers respectively). Through extensive experiments, we further demonstrate that these massive values play a critical role in interpreting contextual knowledge (knowledge obtained from the current context window) rather than in retrieving parametric knowledge stored within the model's parameters. Our further investigation of quantization strategies reveals that ignoring these massive values leads to a pronounced drop in performance on tasks requiring rich contextual understanding, aligning with our analysis. Finally, we trace the emergence of concentrated massive values and find that such concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE), which has appeared since the first layers. These findings shed new light on how Q and K operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization. The Code is Available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Rope_with_LLM.

papers.title: Mary, the Cheeseburger-Eating Vegetarian: Do LLMs Recognize Incoherence in Narratives?
papers.research_question: Are LLMs able to reliably recognize coherence in narratives? We investigate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) can reliably separate incoherent and coherent stories.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations can distinguish incoherent from coherent narratives at the point of incoherence, but their explicit behavioral judgments fail to do so reliably, indicating a gap between internal sensitivity and explicit understanding of narrative coherence.
papers.conclusion: LLMs lack a robust coherence-monitoring process during narrative comprehension, as internal sensitivity to incoherence is not reliably expressed in explicit judgments and decays by the story's end.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' internal representations (perplexity and probing) can distinguish incoherent from coherent narratives at the point of incoherence.
LLMs' explicit ratings (coherence and quality) fail to reliably separate coherent and incoherent narratives.
Reasoning models (with thought strings) do not eliminate these deficits.
LLMs are more sensitive to event-setting incoherence than trait-behavior incoherence, unlike humans.
The separation between coherent and incoherent narratives in internal representations largely disappears by the end of the story.
papers.limitation:
The narratives are from psychological studies rather than naturally occurring stories, and the dataset is limited in size and hand-crafted.
The analysis does not investigate proprietary models, only open-source ones, and results may not generalize broadly.
future_direction: Disentangling unexpectedness and incoherence in LLMs.
Investigating how LLMs respond to event-setting conflicts in fantasy worlds with narrative-specific rules.
papers.abstract: Leveraging a dataset of paired narratives, we investigate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) can reliably separate incoherent and coherent stories. A probing study finds that LLMs' internal representations can reliably identify incoherent narratives. However, LLMs generate responses to rating questions that fail to satisfactorily separate the coherent and incoherent narratives across several prompt variations, hinting at a gap in LLM's understanding of storytelling. The reasoning LLMs tested do not eliminate these deficits, indicating that thought strings may not be able to fully address the discrepancy between model internal state and behavior. Additionally, we find that LLMs appear to be more sensitive to incoherence resulting from an event that violates the setting (e.g., a rainy day in the desert) than to incoherence arising from a character violating an established trait (e.g., Mary, a vegetarian, later orders a cheeseburger), suggesting that LLMs may rely more on prototypical world knowledge than building meaning-based narrative coherence. The consistent asymmetry found in our results suggests that LLMs do not have a complete grasp on narrative coherence.

papers.title: Causal interventions expose implicit situation models for commonsense language understanding
papers.research_question: How do transformer models construct implicit situation models to guide pronoun resolution in commonsense language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a circuit of attention heads responsible for propagating contextual information in transformer models for pronoun resolution, using causal interventions and controlled datasets.
papers.conclusion: The study provides preliminary evidence for distinct neural pathways underlying implicit situation models in transformer models, highlighting the value of causal interventions for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small circuit of attention heads propagates information from context words to guide pronoun resolution.
Syntax-based pronoun resolution uses more localized pathways compared to context-based resolution involving situation models.
Larger models like ALBERT-xxlarge show better performance and more distinct circuits for situation models.
papers.limitation: Single-site interchange interventions may over-count synergies and under-count redundancies in circuits.
future_direction: Explore settings requiring richer interpretations beyond pronoun resolution.
Use chain-of-thought prompting to expose situation models more explicitly in auto-regressive models.
papers.abstract: Accounts of human language processing have long appealed to implicit ``situation models'' that enrich comprehension with relevant but unstated world knowledge. Here, we apply causal intervention techniques to recent transformer models to analyze performance on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), where a single context cue shifts interpretation of an ambiguous pronoun. We identify a relatively small circuit of attention heads that are responsible for propagating information from the context word that guides which of the candidate noun phrases the pronoun ultimately attends to. We then compare how this circuit behaves in a closely matched ``syntactic'' control where the situation model is not strictly necessary. These analyses suggest distinct pathways through which implicit situation models are constructed to guide pronoun resolution.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Functional Abstraction of Knowledge Recall in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the knowledge recall mechanism in large language models be abstracted into a functional structure, and how can this perspective be used to improve knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a functional abstraction of knowledge recall in LLMs, showing that hidden activation vectors correspond to independent functional components (input, function body, return value). This perspective is used to improve contextual knowledge editing via activation patching.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge recall process in LLMs can be abstracted as a functional structure with localized activation vectors serving as independent components, and this abstraction enables more effective knowledge editing through activation patching.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-aware activation vectors are localized to specific token positions and layers: subject and relation vectors in early layers within their token ranges, object vectors in late layers at the final token.
These localized activation vectors function as independent components (input argument, function body, return value) in the knowledge recall process.
Activation interchange experiments show that subject, relation, and object vectors can be swapped independently, supporting the functional abstraction.
The proposed knowledge-scoring algorithm based on activation patching can accurately identify these functional components.
Applying this functional perspective via activation patching improves the efficacy of contextual knowledge editing prompts.
papers.limitation:
The proposed knowledge scoring algorithm relies on a brute-force search method, resulting in high time complexity.
The framework awaits validation on text-generation and general question-answering tasks that specifically involve knowledge recall.
The accuracy of the proposed knowledge editing method requires improvement, suggesting representation rewriting does not fully encapsulate the original knowledge.
future_direction: Developing more efficient knowledge exploration algorithms.
Validating the framework on text-generation and general question-answering tasks.
Deeper exploration of the knowledge storage mechanisms within LLMs.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained transformer large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong knowledge recall capabilities. This paper investigates the knowledge recall mechanism in LLMs by abstracting it into a functional structure. We propose that during knowledge recall, the model's hidden activation space implicitly entails a function execution process where specific activation vectors align with functional components (Input argument, Function body, and Return values). Specifically, activation vectors of relation-related tokens define a mapping function from subjects to objects, with subject-related token activations serving as input arguments and object-related token activations as return values. For experimental verification, we first design a patching-based knowledge-scoring algorithm to identify knowledge-aware activation vectors as independent functional components. Then, we conduct counter-knowledge testing to examine the independent functional effects of each component on knowledge recall outcomes. From this functional perspective, we improve the contextual knowledge editing approach augmented by activation patching. By rewriting incoherent activations in context, we enable improved short-term memory retention for new knowledge prompting.

papers.title: Sparks of Rationality: Do Reasoning LLMs Align with Human Judgment and Choice?
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs exhibit human-like rational deliberation and emotion-driven biases in decision-making.
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning LLMs show higher compliance with rational choice axioms and are more sensitive to emotional steering, with in-context priming producing extreme shifts and representation-level steering yielding more human-like but less reliable effects.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes a reproducible foundation for the scientific study of emotion, reasoning, and choice in LLMs, with implications for auditing and shaping LLM decision-making in real deployments.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking LLMs consistently elicit higher levels of rationality compared to non-thinking models.
In the absence of explicit task instructions, thinking models default to maximizing expected gains as prescribed by Expected Utility Theory.
Thinking models are more faithful at reproducing emotion-linked behavioral shifts directionally aligned with humans.
In-context priming induces strong directional shifts that are often extreme and difficult to calibrate.
Representation-level steering produces more psychologically plausible patterns but with lower reliability.
papers.limitation:
In-context priming induces strong directional shifts that are often extreme and difficult to calibrate.
Representation-level steering produces more psychologically plausible patterns but with lower reliability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly positioned as decision engines for hiring, healthcare, and economic judgment, yet real-world human judgment reflects a balance between rational deliberation and emotion-driven bias. If LLMs are to participate in high-stakes decisions or serve as models of human behavior, it is critical to assess whether they exhibit analogous patterns of (ir)rationalities and biases. To this end, we evaluate multiple LLM families on (i) benchmarks testing core axioms of rational choice and (ii) classic decision domains from behavioral economics and social norms where emotions are known to shape judgment and choice. Across settings, we show that deliberate "thinking" reliably improves rationality and pushes models toward expected-value maximization. To probe human-like affective distortions and their interaction with reasoning, we use two emotion-steering methods: in-context priming (ICP) and representation-level steering (RLS). ICP induces strong directional shifts that are often extreme and difficult to calibrate, whereas RLS produces more psychologically plausible patterns but with lower reliability. Our results suggest that the same mechanisms that improve rationality also amplify sensitivity to affective interventions, and that different steering methods trade off controllability against human-aligned behavior. Overall, this points to a tension between reasoning and affective steering, with implications for both human simulation and the safe deployment of LLM-based decision systems.

papers.title: Trustworthy Reasoning: Evaluating and Enhancing Factual Accuracy in LLM Intermediate Thought Processes
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework addressing a critical vulnerability in Large Language Models (LLMs): the prevalence of factual inaccuracies within intermediate reasoning steps despite correct final answers. This phenomenon poses substantial risks in high-stakes domains including healthcare, legal analysis, and scientific research, where erroneous yet confidently presented reasoning can mislead users into dangerous decisions. Our framework integrates three core components: (1) a specialized fact-checking classifier trained on counterfactually augmented data to detect subtle factual inconsistencies within reasoning chains; (2) an enhanced Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reinforcement learning approach that balances factuality, coherence, and structural correctness through multi-dimensional rewards; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability method examining how factuality improvements manifest in model activations during reasoning processes. Extensive evaluation across multi state-of-the-art models reveals concerning patterns: even leading models like Claude-3.7 and GPT-o1 demonstrate reasoning factual accuracy of only 81.93% and 82.57% respectively. Our approach significantly enhances factual robustness (up to 49.90% improvement) while maintaining or improving performance on challenging benchmarks including Math-500, AIME-2024, and GPQA. Furthermore, our neural activation-level analysis provides actionable insights into how factual enhancements reshape reasoning trajectories within model architectures, establishing foundations for future training methodologies that explicitly target factual robustness through activation-guided optimization.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: Racing Thoughts: Explaining Contextualization Errors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes contextualization errors in large language models, and can they be explained by race conditions in the model's processing layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the LLM Race Conditions Hypothesis to explain contextualization errors in LLMs, providing correlational and causal evidence through mechanistic interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The LLM Race Conditions Hypothesis explains contextualization errors in LLMs, and inference-time interventions can address them, pointing towards potential architectural solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Injecting distractor text into prompts causes sharp performance degradations in contextualization tasks.
There exists a critical window in middle layers where question tokens integrate information from subject entities.
Model failures are driven by unfinished contextualization of subject entities before this critical window.
Patching interventions such as cross-patching and backpatching can improve performance by addressing race conditions.
Race conditions are endemic to feedforward language models, suggesting architectural limitations.
papers.limitation: Does not comprehensively explain all LLM contextualization errors, such as those due to missing factual knowledge.
future_direction: Explore recurrent connections in models to allow later layer representations to influence earlier ones.
Develop more advanced inference-time interventions based on the findings.
papers.abstract: The profound success of transformer-based language models can largely be attributed to their ability to integrate relevant contextual information from an input sequence in order to generate a response or complete a task. However, we know very little about the algorithms that a model employs to implement this capability, nor do we understand their failure modes. For example, given the prompt "John is going fishing, so he walks over to the bank. Can he make an ATM transaction?", a model may incorrectly respond "Yes" if it has not properly contextualized "bank" as a geographical feature, rather than a financial institution. We propose the LLM Race Conditions Hypothesis as an explanation of contextualization errors of this form. This hypothesis identifies dependencies between tokens (e.g., "bank" must be properly contextualized before the final token, "?", integrates information from "bank"), and claims that contextualization errors are a result of violating these dependencies. Using a variety of techniques from mechanistic intepretability, we provide correlational and causal evidence in support of the hypothesis, and suggest inference-time interventions to address it.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Optimal ablation for interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we better quantify the importance of model components for interpretability by using an ablation method that minimizes expected loss?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces optimal ablation (OA), a method for ablating model components by setting them to a constant that minimizes expected loss, leading to better component importance estimates and improved performance in circuit discovery, factual recall localization, and latent prediction.
papers.conclusion: Optimal ablation is a theoretically and empirically better method for ablating model components, improving component importance quantification and downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
OA provides a theoretically grounded way to measure component importance by minimizing spoofing effects.
OA yields lower ablation loss gaps compared to prior methods like zero, mean, resample, and counterfactual ablation.
OA improves circuit discovery, producing smaller and lower-loss circuits.
OA improves causal tracing for factual recall, providing more precise localization.
OA improves latent prediction via OCA lens, achieving better predictive power and causal faithfulness.
papers.limitation: OA requires optimizing constants for each component and subtask, which can be computationally expensive.
future_direction: More efficient optimization methods for OA constants
Scaling interpretability techniques to larger models
papers.abstract: Interpretability studies often involve tracing the flow of information through machine learning models to identify specific model components that perform relevant computations for tasks of interest. Prior work quantifies the importance of a model component on a particular task by measuring the impact of performing ablation on that component, or simulating model inference with the component disabled. We propose a new method, optimal ablation (OA), and show that OA-based component importance has theoretical and empirical advantages over measuring importance via other ablation methods. We also show that OA-based component importance can benefit several downstream interpretability tasks, including circuit discovery, localization of factual recall, and latent prediction.

papers.title: Abstraction in time: Finding hierarchical linguistic structure in a model of relational processing
papers.research_question: Does the oscillatory activation in LISA/DORA models during processing match human cortical activity during language processing, suggesting a common mechanism for hierarchical representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LISA/DORA models of relational processing exhibit oscillatory activation patterns during sentence processing that closely match human cortical tracking of hierarchical linguistic structures, suggesting that mechanisms for relational binding may underlie language representation.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that abstract hierarchical linguistic representations can be processed by models of relational reasoning, and suggests that integrating such models with language processing models could advance cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LISA/DORA models parse English sentences and show firing patterns that mirror cortical activity observed in Ding et al. (2016), with activation bursts at sentence (1Hz), phrasal (2Hz), and syllabic (4Hz) rates.
The models' binding mechanisms, using temporal synchrony and asynchrony, naturally produce hierarchical representations similar to those in human language processing.
These models, built for analogy and relational learning, generalize to language processing without modification, unlike grammar-based or statistical models.
The results support the idea that relational role representation may be a foundation for human cognitive capacities like language.
Integrating models of relational reasoning and language processing could lead to more plausible cognitive models.
future_direction: Testing on natural speech input
Testing on varied syntactic structures
Testing in rich discourse contexts and multilingual input
papers.abstract: Abstract mental representation is fundamental for human cognition. Forming such representations in time, especially from dynamic and noisy perceptual input, is a challenge for any processing modality, but perhaps none so acutely as for language processing. We show that LISA (Hummel & Holyaok, 1997) and DORA (Doumas, Hummel, & Sandhofer, 2008), models built to process and to learn structured (i.e., symbolic) rep resentations of conceptual properties and relations from unstructured inputs, show oscillatory activation during processing that is highly similar to the cortical activity elicited by the linguistic stimuli from Ding et al.(2016). We argue, as Ding et al.(2016), that this activation reflects formation of hierarchical linguistic representation, and furthermore, that the kind of computational mechanisms in LISA/DORA (e.g., temporal binding by systematic asynchrony of firing) may underlie formation of abstract linguistic representations in the human brain. It may be this repurposing that allowed for the generation or mergence of hierarchical linguistic structure, and therefore, human language, from extant cognitive and neural systems. We conclude that models of thinking and reasoning and models of language processing must be integrated —not only for increased plausiblity, but in order to advance both fields towards a larger integrative model of human cognition

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
